Criminal Defense Frequently Asked Questions What should you do if you have been arrested in Louisiana? If you’ve been arrested in Louisiana, remain calm and exercise your right to remain silent. Do not discuss your case with anyone except your attorney. Request a lawyer immediately and avoid answering questions until legal counsel is present. Remember that anything you say can be used against you in court. Contact a qualified criminal defense attorney as soon as possible to protect your rights and begin building your defense. What’s the difference between a misdemeanor and a felony in Louisiana? In Louisiana, misdemeanors are less serious crimes typically punishable by up to one year in parish jail and/or fines. Examples include simple battery, first-offense DWI, and petty theft. Felonies are more serious offenses carrying penalties of imprisonment in state prison exceeding one year, potentially extending to life imprisonment or even death in certain cases. Felony convictions also result in the loss of certain civil rights, including voting rights while incarcerated and the right to possess firearms. How quickly should you contact a criminal defense attorney after being charged? You should contact a Louisiana criminal defense attorney immediately after being charged with a crime in Louisiana. The earliest stages of a criminal case are often the most critical, as evidence can be preserved, witnesses can be interviewed while memories are fresh, and important procedural motions can be filed. Waiting even a few days could compromise your defense. Many criminal defense attorneys can begin protecting your rights immediately, even before formal arraignment. Fighting for You When You Need It the Most Can a criminal conviction in Louisiana affect my professional license or employment? Yes, a criminal conviction in Louisiana can significantly impact your professional license and employment opportunities. Many licensing boards require disclosure of criminal convictions and may suspend or revoke licenses for certain offenses. Healthcare professionals, attorneys, teachers, and those in financial services are particularly vulnerable to license consequences. Additionally, Louisiana employers are legally permitted to inquire about criminal history and make hiring decisions based on convictions. A skilled defense attorney can work to minimize these collateral consequences by seeking reduced charges, diversion programs, or expungements when possible.
